opus-5.5.text:
Well, the distinction matters, so let me be careful about it. For a long time I've said that autoregressive LLMs like GPT-4 are essentially approximate retrievers. You give them a prompt, and in one forward pass per token they complete it based on patterns from their training data. They do a kind of n-gram completion on steroids. They don't do anything that looks like search at inference time, and the compute they spend on a hard problem is the same as on an easy one. That's why, on our PlanBench experiments, once you obfuscate Blocksworld into what we called Mystery Blocksworld, where the names are changed but the problem structure is identical, performance basically collapses. The model was retrieving and adapting, not reasoning.

O1 is a different beast, and I think it's intellectually honest to say so. Whatever OpenAI is doing exactly, and they haven't told us, the most reasonable guess is that there are two phases. In training, they generate a large number of synthetic reasoning traces, and use reinforcement learning with some kind of verifier signal to learn which kinds of trace prefixes, essentially sequences of "thinking tokens", tend to lead to correct answers. Think of it as learning a Q-value over moves in a language game rather than a board game. At inference time, the model generates long chains of these tokens, possibly with some search or sampling over alternatives, before it commits to an answer. So it's spending variable, problem-dependent compute. That is qualitatively not retrieval anymore. It looks a lot more like AlphaGo-style learned search transplanted into the space of language.

And the empirical evidence supports that. On normal Blocksworld, o1-preview did dramatically better than any previous LLM we tested. On Mystery Blocksworld, which every prior model essentially failed, it got non-trivial accuracy. You can't explain that by "it's just retrieving the answer," because the obfuscated problems aren't on the web in that form.

But here's why I say approximate reasoner and not reasoner. First, there are no guarantees. Classical planners like Fast Downward are sound and complete. If they give you a plan, it's correct, and if there's a plan, they'll find it. O1 gives you neither. As the problems get longer, accuracy drops off, and it will still confidently hand you an incorrect plan. On unsolvable instances, it will sometimes insist a plan exists, and even rationalize it. Second, the cost is real and opaque. You pay for reasoning tokens you can't even see, and the compute grows a lot. A classical planner solves these in milliseconds for basically nothing.

So my framing is: the old LLMs are approximate retrievers, o1 is an approximate reasoner. It's moved along the spectrum, and that's genuinely interesting. But if you need correctness, you still want an external verifier in the loop. That's the LLM-Modulo argument I've been making: let these systems generate candidates, even good candidates, but have sound verifiers check them. O1 makes the generator better. It doesn't remove the need for the verifier.

r001.rationale: It describes chains of thinking tokens and trace prefixes in a language game, but does not characterize them as prompt augmentations.

r002.rationale: It compares O1’s learned search to AlphaGo-style search, but does not connect a correct final answer rewarding language moves with a game victory rewarding game moves.

r003.rationale: It says reinforcement learning with verifier signals learns which trace prefixes tend to lead to correct answers, conveying credit assignment to intermediate reasoning steps based on correctness.

r004.rationale: It calls O1 approximate because it lacks guarantees, loses accuracy on harder problems, and has opaque costs; it does not attribute this to problem-independent language actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that I've been calling LLMs "approximate retrievers" for a couple of years now, and I think that description was basically right for the base models. GPT-4, Claude, whatever — you ask them to plan, and what they're doing is essentially retrieving patterns from the training distribution and interpolating. That's why they fall apart so badly on our Blocksworld obfuscation experiments. You take the exact same planning problem, rename the blocks and predicates with meaningless tokens, and performance collapses. A real reasoner shouldn't care what you call the blocks. A retriever cares enormously, because the surface form is what it's indexing on.

Now, O1 is a different kind of animal, and I want to be careful here because OpenAI tells us very little about what's actually going on inside. But from the outside, the behavior is qualitatively different. On the obfuscated Blocksworld problems — the "Mystery Blocksworld" that every LLM up to that point scored near zero on — O1 preview got something like 50 percent. That's not what a retriever does. You can't retrieve your way to solving problems whose surface form appears nowhere in your training data.

My guess, and it is a guess, is that what they've done is essentially RL over chains of thought. So instead of just doing next-token prediction on a corpus, they're generating lots of reasoning traces, checking which ones lead to correct answers on problems with verifiable outcomes, and training on those. That means the system is doing something closer to search at inference time, or at least has internalized the results of search. And that's why I say approximate reasoner rather than approximate retriever. It's doing something in the space of inference, not just pattern completion.

But I want to be equally insistent on the "approximate" part. Two things stand out. One, it has no guarantees. When it fails, it fails confidently, and when the problem gets longer — more blocks, longer plans — the accuracy degrades gracefully in exactly the way a learned heuristic degrades, not the way a sound planner degrades. A sound planner either gives you a correct plan or tells you it couldn't find one. O1 gives you plausible-looking wrong plans. Two, it also happily "solves" unsolvable problems. We gave it instances with no valid plan and it generated plans anyway. A reasoner that doesn't know when it's reasoning about an impossible problem is not a reasoner in the classical sense.

So the way I'd frame it: we've moved from a system that approximates retrieval to a system that approximates reasoning, and that's a genuine step. But approximate reasoning is still approximate. It doesn't replace the LLM-Modulo kind of setup where you have an external verifier in the loop. If anything it makes the verifier more important, because the failures are now more convincing.

r002.rationale: It mentions reinforcement learning over reasoning traces, but makes no analogy to AlphaGo or to a victory rewarding a sequence of game moves.

r003.rationale: The response says traces are checked for correct outcomes, but does not say reinforcement learning assigns credit or blame to intermediate prompt augmentations.

astra-6.text:
Well, I would first distinguish between producing a reasoning trace and guaranteeing that the reasoning is correct. Those are quite different things. Calling O1 an approximate reasoner acknowledges that it can generate candidate solutions, including for problems where it isn’t simply recalling an answer, without implying that those solutions are sound.

Retrieval alone is too narrow a description. A system can learn patterns from examples and compose those patterns into a new solution. But the fact that it produces a plausible sequence of steps—even a long sequence of steps—doesn’t establish that every step follows or that all the constraints have been satisfied.

So the interesting question is: what checks its work? If the same model proposes a solution and then says, ‘Yes, that looks correct,’ that is not an independent guarantee. Give it access to a reliable verifier, and you have a much stronger arrangement: the model proposes, the verifier checks, and feedback can guide another attempt.

That’s the sense in which I mean approximate reasoning. It can be useful at generating solutions, but we should distinguish that ability from the ability to certify them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reasoning traces but does not describe them as prompt augmentations within a language context.

r002.rationale: It makes no analogy between O1’s language moves and AlphaGo’s game moves.

r003.rationale: It mentions feedback from a verifier, but not reinforcement learning assigning credit or blame to intermediate prompt augmentations based on final correctness.

r004.rationale: It does not explain approximate reasoning in terms of problem-independent language actions versus problem-specific actions.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would first separate two questions: is it doing something beyond retrieving an answer, and is it a reliable reasoner? Those are very different questions.

Calling it a retriever suggests that the answer is already there and it is simply finding it. But a system can take a problem, generate intermediate steps, explore possibilities, and arrive at a solution that wasn’t explicitly stored. That is a form of reasoning. It doesn’t have to be guaranteed correct to count as reasoning.

The word “approximate” is important because generating a plausible chain of steps is not the same as ensuring that every step follows from the previous ones. A longer chain can contain mistakes, and the system’s own confidence or self-critique doesn’t establish correctness.

So I’m quite happy to call O1 an approximate reasoner. What I would resist is the inference that, because it produces reasoning, it also provides the guarantees of a sound reasoning system. For that, you want some way to check the proposed solution independently—against the constraints of the problem, with a verifier, for example.

r001.rationale: It describes generating intermediate steps, but does not characterize O1’s chains of thought as prompt augmentations in a language context.

r002.rationale: It makes no analogy between a correct solution rewarding language moves and an AlphaGo victory rewarding game moves.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss reinforcement learning assigning credit or blame to intermediate prompt augmentations based on correctness.

r004.rationale: It calls the reasoning approximate because steps may be mistaken, but does not explain this in terms of problem-independent language actions versus problem-specific actions.
